Ensemble Routing for Prompt-Adaptive Cost-Aware LLM Inference

DOI: XXXXXXX.XXXXXXXConference: The ACM Web Conference 2027; May 10–14, 2027; Dublin, Ireland4320
Saul Urso1,3, Emanuele Carlini1, Patrizio Dazzi1,3, Matteo Mordacchini2 Affiliation: 1Institute of Information Science and Technologies, CNR, Italy
2Institute of Informatics and Telematics, CNR, Italy
3University of Pisa, Department of Computer Science, Italy email: saul.urso@phd.unipi.it, emanuele.carlini@isti.cnr.it, patrizio.dazzi@unipi.it, matteo.mordacchini@iit.cnr.it
2026
Abstract.

Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support Web-based services that must balance response quality and inference cost across heterogeneous requests. Conventional routing selects one model per prompt, while fixed ensembles cannot adapt their composition and cost to individual requests. We introduce PISA, a prompt-adaptive, cost-aware single-model router, and PISA-E, its extension to ensemble routing. At the core of both methods, PISA combines soft cluster memberships with model-specific predictors to estimate individual model capabilities. Building on these estimates, PISA-E jointly selects ensemble composition and cardinality under an explicit cost–quality preference that can be adjusted at inference time without retraining. A tractable ensemble-success surrogate and efficient candidate selection enable this extension without ensemble-specific training. Across four LLM routing benchmarks under in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions, PISA achieves the highest macro-average cost–performance hypervolume among the evaluated single-model routers in both settings. Meanwhile, PISA-E achieves the highest macro-average task performance among the evaluated ensemble approaches when prioritizing response quality, surpassing the strongest competitors by 2.09 and 2.87 percentage points under ID and OOD conditions, respectively. At selected lower-cost operating points, it also exceeds the strongest ensemble competitors’ macro-average task performance while reducing average inference cost by approximately 36% and 25%, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of prompt-adaptive capability estimation for both single-model routing and selective ensembling.

Keywords: 
Large Language Models, LLM Routing, Cost–Aware Inference, LLM Ensembling

1. Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in Web-based services, supporting applications such as search and information discovery, recommendation, and intelligent agents (Hui et al., 2026; Behdin et al., 2025). Their adoption also extends to publicly accessible LLM services, creating new challenges for efficient and scalable inference (Liu et al., 2026b). These services must handle heterogeneous user requests while balancing response quality and inference cost. When multiple LLMs with different capabilities and pricing structures are available, invoking expensive models indiscriminately wastes resources, whereas consistently selecting inexpensive models can compromise response quality. Moreover, different users and requests may have different cost preferences, making it desirable to adapt inference strategies to both prompt characteristics and inference-cost preferences (Varangot-Reille et al., 2026).

LLM routing addresses this challenge by selecting models according to prompt characteristics, expected response quality, and inference cost (Moslem and Kelleher, 2026). Recent approaches extend routing to budget-adaptive selection (Zu et al., 2026), reasoning-strategy selection (Pan et al., 2026), and additional deployment constraints (Li et al., 2026b). However, selecting a single model cannot exploit the complementary capabilities of multiple LLMs. Ensembling offers an alternative by combining multiple model responses (Chen et al., 2026), but introduces additional inference costs. Existing ensemble approaches explore adaptive model composition, diversity-aware selection, and budget-constrained optimization (Huang et al., 2024; Cohen et al., 2026; Tekin et al., 2024). Nevertheless, existing approaches typically address only parts of the problem: some adapt ensemble composition without explicitly optimizing inference cost, while others rely on classification-specific aggregation or sequential execution. Moreover, ensemble cardinality is generally fixed during training or configuration, limiting the ability to adjust the number of invoked models to individual prompts and changing cost preferences at inference time. This motivates ensemble routing, where both the composition and cardinality of the invoked model subset are determined dynamically at inference time according to prompt characteristics and an explicit cost–quality preference.

We introduce PISA , a prompt-adaptive, cost-aware single-model router that estimates the capabilities of individual LLMs, and PISA-E , its extension to prompt-adaptive ensemble routing. PISA-E reuses the individual capability estimates to construct a tractable surrogate for ensemble success, eliminating the need to train separate quality estimators for different model combinations. By combining these estimates with inference cost, PISA-E selects prompt-specific model subsets, jointly determining which models to invoke and how many. Crucially, the cost–quality preference can be adjusted at inference time without additional hyperparameter optimization or retraining, allowing the same framework to support different operating points. The selected responses are combined through capability-weighted semantic similarity to produce the final ensemble response.

We evaluate PISA and PISA-E on four LLM routing benchmarks under in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions. PISA achieves the highest macro-average hypervolume among the evaluated single-model routers in both settings, ranking first in six of the eight benchmark–setting combinations. PISA-E achieves the highest macro-average task performance among the evaluated ensemble approaches in both settings, improving over the strongest competitors by 2.09 percentage points under ID and 2.87 under OOD conditions when prioritizing response quality. At selected lower-cost operating points, it also exceeds the strongest competitors’ macro-average task performance while reducing average inference cost by approximately 36% and 25%, respectively. Finally, comparisons with fixed-cardinality variants demonstrate the benefits of adapting ensemble size to individual prompts.

Our main contributions are:

  • •

    We develop PISA, a prompt-adaptive, cost-aware single-model router that estimates individual model capabilities through soft cluster memberships and model-specific predictors, providing the foundation for ensemble routing.

  • •

    We propose PISA-E, a framework for prompt-adaptive, cost-aware ensemble routing that uses ensemble-level utility estimates derived from individual model capabilities to jointly determine ensemble composition and cardinality at inference time, according to prompt characteristics and inference-cost preferences.

  • •

    We evaluate both methods across four benchmarks under ID and OOD conditions, demonstrating the highest macro-average single-model routing HV and ensemble task performance among the evaluated approaches in both settings. We also demonstrate operating points with higher task performance at lower cost than the strongest ensemble competitors and quantify the benefits of prompt-dependent ranking and adaptive ensemble cardinality.

2. Problem Formulation

Let ℳ={1,…,M}\mathcal{M}=\{1,\ldots,M\} denote a fixed pool of candidate LLMs. Given a prompt qq, model routing selects one or more models from ℳ\mathcal{M} while trading off response quality and inference cost.

For each model m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M}, let Xm​(q)∈{0,1}X_{m}(q)\in\{0,1\} indicate whether the model produces a correct answer, with prompt-dependent probability

(1) pm​(q)=Pr⁡(Xm​(q)=1∣q).p_{m}(q)=\Pr\!\left(X_{m}(q)=1\mid q\right).

Since pm​(q)p_{m}(q) is unknown at inference time, a router operates on an estimate p^m​(q)\hat{p}_{m}(q). Let c¯m​(q)∈[0,1]\bar{c}_{m}(q)\in[0,1] denote the normalized cost of querying model mm on prompt qq.

2.1. Cost-Aware Single-Model Routing

Standard model routing selects exactly one model for each prompt. We formulate the cost-aware routing decision as

(2) m^​(q)=arg​maxm∈ℳ⁡Jm​(q,α),\hat{m}(q)=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{m\in\mathcal{M}}J_{m}(q;\alpha),

where

(3) Jm​(q,α)=α​p^m​(q)+(1−α)​(1−c¯m​(q)),α∈[0,1].J_{m}(q;\alpha)=\alpha\hat{p}_{m}(q)+(1-\alpha)\left(1-\bar{c}_{m}(q)\right),\qquad\alpha\in[0,1].

Here, α\alpha controls the trade-off between predicted response quality and inference cost.

2.2. Cost-Aware Ensemble Routing

We generalize standard routing by allowing the router to select any non-empty subset E⊆ℳ,E≠∅E\subseteq\mathcal{M},E\neq\emptyset. All models in EE are queried, and their outputs are combined by a response resolver 𝒜\mathcal{A}, which may implement any suitable aggregation strategy. If Ym​(q)Y_{m}(q) denotes the output of model mm, the resulting ensemble output is

(4) YE​(q)=𝒜⁡({Ym​(q):m∈E}).Y_{E}(q)=\mathcal{A}\!\left(\{Y_{m}(q):m\in E\}\right).

Let

(5) XE​(q)=[YE​(q)​ is correct],X_{E}(q)=\mathds{1}\!\left[Y_{E}(q)\text{ is correct}\right],

and define the corresponding probability of correctness as

(6) pE​(q)=Pr⁡(XE​(q)=1∣q).p_{E}(q)=\Pr\!\left(X_{E}(q)=1\mid q\right).

As in the single-model setting, pE​(q)p_{E}(q) is unavailable at inference time; we denote its router-provided estimate by p^E​(q)\hat{p}_{E}(q). Let C¯​(E,q)∈[0,1]\bar{C}(E,q)\in[0,1] denote the normalized inference cost associated with querying ensemble EE. Cost-aware ensemble routing then solves

(7) E^​(q)=arg​max∅≠E⊆ℳ⁡JE​(q,α),\hat{E}(q)=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\emptyset\neq E\subseteq\mathcal{M}}J_{E}(q;\alpha),

with

(8) JE​(q,α)=α​p^E​(q)+(1−α)​(1−C¯​(E,q)).J_{E}(q;\alpha)=\alpha\hat{p}_{E}(q)+(1-\alpha)\left(1-\bar{C}(E,q)\right).

Single-model routing is recovered by restricting the feasible ensembles to singletons, |E|=1|E|=1. Thus, the two settings differ only in their action spaces: standard routing selects an element of ℳ\mathcal{M}, whereas ensemble routing selects an element of 2ℳ∖{∅}2^{\mathcal{M}}\setminus\{\emptyset\}.

Solving this problem requires estimating the expected quality and inference cost of candidate model subsets. Section 3 describes how we instantiate these quantities and perform cost-aware model and ensemble selection.

3. Methodology

Our approach builds on a shared capability-estimation framework to support both single-model and ensemble routing. PISA estimates the prompt-dependent capabilities of individual LLMs and uses them for cost-aware single-model selection. PISA-E extends this framework to ensemble routing by combining the same capability estimates into an ensemble-success surrogate, allowing model subsets of different compositions and cardinalities to be evaluated under the cost–quality objective introduced in Section 2. Figure 1 illustrates the resulting inference pipeline.

3.1. PISA: Model Routing via Soft Assignments

The first stage estimates how likely each candidate model is to produce a correct response to a given prompt. PISA learns prompt-dependent capability estimates from historical model outcomes and semantic representations of the input queries. Assume a training set of NN prompts, where each prompt qiq_{i} is represented by an embedding xi=f⁡(qi)∈ℝdx_{i}=f(q_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and is associated with a correctness score si​m∈[0,1]s_{im}\in[0,1] for each model m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M}. At inference time, only the embedding x=f⁡(q)x=f(q) of the incoming prompt is available.

To capture similarities among prompts, we partition the fit-set embeddings using X-means, which determines both the number of clusters KK and their centroids. PISA represents each query through soft memberships over the learned centroids, allowing its representation to incorporate information from multiple clusters. After ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalizing embeddings and centroids, these memberships are computed from cosine distances as

(9) uk​(x)=exp⁡(−β​dk​(x))∑j=1Kexp⁡(−β​dj​(x)),dk​(x)=1−x⊤​μk,u_{k}(x)=\frac{\exp(-\beta d_{k}(x))}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(-\beta d_{j}(x))},\qquad d_{k}(x)=1-x^{\top}\mu_{k},

where μk\mu_{k} denotes the centroid of cluster kk and β>0\beta>0 controls the concentration of the assignments. This representation allows capability estimation to exploit information from multiple neighboring regions instead of relying on a single hard assignment.

Using the resulting membership vector u⁡(x)u(x), PISA learns an independent logistic predictor for each candidate model. Each predictor is trained using the soft memberships of the training prompts and their corresponding binary correctness labels, obtained by thresholding evaluation scores at 0.50.5. For an incoming prompt, the estimated capability of model mm is

(10) p^m​(x)=σ⁡(wm⊤​u​(x)+bm),\hat{p}_{m}(x)=\sigma\!\left(w_{m}^{\top}u(x)+b_{m}\right),

where σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) is the logistic sigmoid and (wm,bm)(w_{m},b_{m}) are the parameters fitted for model mm using L2-regularized logistic regression. The regularization strength λm\lambda_{m} is selected independently for each model through 5-fold cross-validation minimizing log loss over 10 logarithmically spaced values between 10−410^{-4} and 10410^{4}. The selected predictor is then refitted on the full training set.

To incorporate inference cost into the routing decision, we estimate each model’s cost from its average observed training-set cost. Let ci​mc_{im} denote the cost of invoking model mm on training prompt qiq_{i}, and define

(11) cmavg=1N​∑i=1Nci​m,c¯m=cmavgmaxm′∈ℳ⁡cm′avg.c_{m}^{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}c_{im},\qquad\bar{c}_{m}=\frac{c_{m}^{\mathrm{avg}}}{\max_{m^{\prime}\in\mathcal{M}}c_{m^{\prime}}^{\mathrm{avg}}}.

The normalized cost c¯m∈[0,1]\bar{c}_{m}\in[0,1] provides the cost term in Eq. (3). For each incoming prompt and cost preference α\alpha, PISA selects the model maximizing the corresponding single-model utility in Eq. (2). The resulting capability estimates also provide the foundation for the ensemble-routing extension described next.

3.2. PISA-E: Prompt-Adaptive Cost-Aware LLM Ensembling

While PISA selects a single model, PISA-E extends the routing decision to model subsets, allowing both ensemble composition and cardinality to vary with the prompt and cost preference. Given the capability estimates {p^m​(x)}m=1M\{\hat{p}_{m}(x)\}_{m=1}^{M}, PISA-E considers ensembles E⊆ℳE\subseteq\mathcal{M} with 1≤|E|≤kmax1\leq|E|\leq k_{\max}, where kmaxk_{\max} denotes the maximum ensemble size. Its central challenge is to evaluate the expected utility of candidate subsets before invoking their constituent models.

Directly estimating the performance of every possible ensemble would require modeling the behavior of numerous model combinations. Instead, PISA-E constructs an ensemble-level utility estimate from the individual capabilities already provided by PISA. Specifically, we use the probability that a strict majority of the selected models produce correct responses as a tractable surrogate for comparing candidate ensembles. This criterion captures how the predicted capabilities of the constituent models combine, without requiring ensemble-specific predictors or observing their generated responses.

For an ensemble EE of size kk, we model the correctness of each constituent model through a Bernoulli variable ZmZ_{m} with success probability p^m​(x)\hat{p}_{m}(x). Assuming conditional independence of these variables given the prompt, the strict-majority success probability is

(12) p^Emaj​(x)=Pr⁡(∑m∈EZm≥⌊k2⌋+1),Zm∼Bernoulli⁡(p^m​(x)),\hat{p}_{E}^{\mathrm{maj}}(x)=\Pr\!\left(\sum_{m\in E}Z_{m}\geq\left\lfloor\frac{k}{2}\right\rfloor+1\right),\quad Z_{m}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\hat{p}_{m}(x)),

with the ZmZ_{m} treated as independent. We compute this probability using the standard Poisson-binomial dynamic program. The strict-majority success probability serves as a surrogate for ensemble selection, since the outcome of the final response resolver also depends on relationships among the generated responses. Accordingly, p^Emaj​(x)\hat{p}^{\mathrm{maj}}_{E}(x) provides the quality term in the ensemble-routing objective independently of the response resolution procedure.

To balance this surrogate with inference cost, PISA-E estimates the cost of an ensemble by summing the average costs of its constituent models. Let the model costs defined in Eq. (11) be ordered as c(1)avg≥⋯≥c(M)avgc_{(1)}^{\mathrm{avg}}\geq\cdots\geq c_{(M)}^{\mathrm{avg}}. We normalize the ensemble cost as

(13) C¯​(E)=∑m∈Ecmavg∑j=1kmaxc(j)avg.\bar{C}(E)=\frac{\sum_{m\in E}c_{m}^{\mathrm{avg}}}{\sum_{j=1}^{k_{\max}}c_{(j)}^{\mathrm{avg}}}.

The denominator corresponds to the maximum cost of any subset containing at most kmaxk_{\max} models and remains constant across candidate ensembles. Combining this normalized cost with the strict-majority surrogate yields the ensemble utility in Eq. (8), allowing subsets of different cardinalities to be compared under the same cost–quality preference.

Since evaluating all feasible subsets would require a combinatorial search, PISA-E uses a greedy candidate-construction procedure. For each prompt, the models are first ranked according to their utilities, using the same cost normalization as for all candidate ensembles:

(14) J{m}​(x,α)=α​p^m​(x)+(1−α)​(1−C¯​({m})).J_{\{m\}}(x;\alpha)=\alpha\hat{p}_{m}(x)+(1-\alpha)\bigl(1-\bar{C}(\{m\})\bigr).

Here, C¯​({m})\bar{C}(\{m\}) is obtained from Eq. (13) with E={m}E=\{m\}, so the cost of each model is normalized by the sum of the kmaxk_{\max} largest average model costs. Candidate ensembles are then constructed as progressively larger prefixes of this ranking, considering odd cardinalities up to kmaxk_{\max}. Each candidate is evaluated using its strict-majority success probability and normalized inference cost, and the ensemble maximizing the resulting utility is selected. For kmax=1k_{\max}=1, both the cost normalization and the selection rule reduce to those of PISA.

Restricting the candidates to odd cardinalities follows directly from the strict-majority surrogate. For any even-cardinality ensemble, removing one constituent model produces an odd-cardinality subset whose strict-majority success probability is at least as high, since the required number of correct models decreases by one. As the subset also incurs lower inference cost, the even-cardinality ensemble cannot achieve higher utility under the surrogate objective. Consequently, considering only odd cardinalities does not exclude an optimal solution to the surrogate-based subset optimization problem. The greedy prefix construction further restricts the search space and does not guarantee the globally optimal subset, but provides an efficient procedure for selecting among candidate ensembles. A comparison with exhaustive surrogate optimization is provided in Appendix E.

Once an ensemble EE has been selected, PISA-E queries its constituent models in parallel and combines their responses through self-weighted BERTScore (Zhang* et al., 2020), a capability-aware extension of minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding. The resolver incorporates the estimated capabilities of both candidate and reference responses, weighting their contributions according to their predicted reliability. Let yiy_{i} denote the response produced by model i∈Ei\in E. We first normalize the capability estimates over the selected ensemble:

(15) wi​(x,E)=p^i​(x)∑j∈Ep^j​(x).w_{i}(x,E)=\frac{\hat{p}_{i}(x)}{\sum_{j\in E}\hat{p}_{j}(x)}.

The score assigned to each candidate response is then

(16) Si​(x,E)=wi​(x,E)​∑j∈Ewj​(x,E)​BERTScore⁡(yi,yj).S_{i}(x,E)=w_{i}(x,E)\sum_{j\in E}w_{j}(x,E)\operatorname{BERTScore}(y_{i},y_{j}).

The final ensemble response is selected as

(17) y∗=arg⁡maxi∈E​Si​(x,E).y^{*}=\arg\max_{i\in E}S_{i}(x,E).

Alternative response resolution strategies are described in Appendix A. Algorithm 1 summarizes the complete inference procedure, from prompt-dependent capability estimation to cost-aware ensemble selection.

4. Experiments

4.1. Experimental Setup

Benchmarks.

We evaluate PISA and PISA-E on four LLM routing benchmarks: LLMRouterBench Track-2 (Li et al., 2026a), RouterBench (Hu et al., 2024), FusionBench (Feng et al., 2026), and SPROUT (Somerstep et al., 2025). These benchmarks cover heterogeneous candidate model pools and task groups, with performance measured using their respective evaluation scores.

Evaluation Protocol.

We consider both ID and OOD evaluations. For ID experiments, we use the released data partitions when available; otherwise, we split the data into 70% development and 30% test, further dividing the development set into 80% training and 20% validation. For OOD experiments, we train exclusively on ID task groups, select configurations using ID validation data, and evaluate on held-out task groups. ID and OOD experiments use separately fitted routers. All experiments are evaluated over five seeds, with fixed data partitions, and all approaches are evaluated using the model responses provided by the benchmarks.

Baselines.

We compare PISA against four single-model routing baselines: EmbedLLM (Zhuang et al., 2025), Avengers-Pro (Zhang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025c), K-NN, and a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). For PISA-E, we consider five LLM ensembling approaches: DFPE (Cohen et al., 2026), LLM-TOPLA (Tekin et al., 2024), SelectLLM (Maurya et al., 2025), PairRanker (Jiang et al., 2023), and BERTScore-based MBR (Zhang* et al., 2020). PairRanker employs PairRM, the pairwise reward model introduced by LLM-Blender, to rank candidate responses. We evaluate its pretrained checkpoint (PairRanker-PT) and a fine-tuned variant (PairRanker-FT), trained following the original procedure.

We additionally report an oracle single-model selector that uses ground-truth evaluation scores to select the best-performing model for each prompt, providing a reference for the performance attainable through perfect model selection.

Metrics.

We report task performance and inference cost, computed from benchmark-specific scores and model invocation costs. Task performance is macro-averaged across task groups. To summarize cost–performance trade-offs, we use normalized dominated hypervolume (HV), multiplied by 100. The reference performance corresponds to a random router, while the reference cost is set to the 40th percentile of the full-pool cost distribution for single-model routing and the 70th percentile for ensemble routing. These reference points are chosen to accommodate all the operating points of the compared methods. Since existing ensemble approaches generally provide a single operating point rather than a cost–performance frontier, we compare them directly in terms of task performance and inference cost.

Implementation.

We employ Qwen3-Embedding-8B (Zhang et al., 2025a) for creating the prompt embeddings required by the routers. PISA-E considers ensembles of up to eleven models. Hyperparameters and ensemble configurations are selected independently for each benchmark using validation task performance at α=1\alpha=1. The same fitted capability estimators are reused across different cost–performance operating points. Further implementation details, including the HV definition, are provided in Appendix A.

4.2. PISA Evaluation

We first evaluate PISA as a single-model router, comparing its cost–performance trade-offs against four established routing baselines. Table 1 reports the HV across four benchmarks under ID and OOD conditions.

PISA achieves the highest macro-average HV among the evaluated routers in both ID and OOD settings, reaching 37.41 and 22.85, respectively, compared with 35.78 and 21.33 for EmbedLLM-MF, the strongest competing router by this measure. PISA ranks first in six of the eight benchmark–setting combinations, showing that its aggregate advantage extends across multiple benchmarks. These results establish PISA as an effective single-model router in its own right, while its capability estimates also provide the foundation for ensemble selection in PISA-E.

4.3. PISA-E Evaluation

We evaluate PISA-E against existing LLM ensembling approaches across the four benchmarks. Tables 2 and 3 report task performance and inference cost under ID and OOD conditions, respectively.

PISA-E attains higher macro-average task performance than the strongest competing ensemble approaches while requiring less inference expenditure. On ID benchmarks, PISA-E at α=0.75\alpha=0.75 achieves 73.78% task performance at a cost of 84×10−484\times 10^{-4} USD/query, compared with 73.18% at 132×10−4132\times 10^{-4} USD/query of the best competitor, SelectLLM. This represents a 0.60 percentage-point improvement with approximately 36% lower cost. Under OOD conditions, PISA-E at α=0.85\alpha=0.85 achieves 60.85% performance at a cost of 292×10−4292\times 10^{-4} USD/query, compared with 60.37% at 387×10−4387\times 10^{-4} USD/query for DFPE, improving performance by 0.48 percentage points while reducing cost by approximately 25%.

When response quality is prioritized (α=1\alpha=1), PISA-E reaches the highest macro-average task performance among the evaluated deployable approaches in both settings, reaching 75.27% on ID benchmarks and 63.24% on OOD benchmarks. These scores exceed those of the strongest competing ensemble approaches by 2.09 and 2.87 percentage points, respectively. Although some competitors achieve higher performance on individual benchmarks, none matches PISA-E in macro-average task performance across either evaluation setting.

Thus, PISA-E supports different cost–performance preferences by varying the trade-off parameter α\alpha. On ID benchmarks, decreasing α\alpha from 1.0 to 0.3 reduces average inference cost by a factor of 21.5, while task performance decreases from 75.27% to 70.75%. On OOD benchmarks, the corresponding cost reduction is approximately 106-fold, with performance decreasing from 63.24% to 50.54%.

Table 4 reports how ensemble cardinality varies with the cost preference α\alpha, together with the proportion of queries assigned to a single model. At α=0.3\alpha=0.3, PISA-E selects a single model for 84.33% of ID queries and 82.41% of OOD queries. Increasing α\alpha leads to larger ensembles on average, with cardinalities reaching 6.42 and 7.39 at α=1.0\alpha=1.0 under ID and OOD conditions, respectively. Even when inference cost is not penalized, however, PISA-E selects a single model for 21.56% of ID queries and 9.31% of OOD queries. Ensemble cardinality therefore remains prompt-dependent even when the selection objective prioritizes response quality exclusively.

4.4. Adaptive vs. Fixed Ensembling

We investigate whether prompt-adaptive ensemble cardinality improves cost–performance trade-offs over fixed-cardinality alternatives. To isolate this effect, we compare PISA-E against variants of the same framework constrained to select exactly kk models per query, with k∈{1,3,5,7,9,11}k\in\{1,3,5,7,9,11\}. In particular, k=1k=1 corresponds to PISA. All variants use the same capability estimates, ensemble-success surrogate, and resolver, while varying α\alpha to obtain different operating points.

Table 5 reports the HV achieved by adaptive and fixed-cardinality selection under ID and OOD conditions. PISA-E achieves the highest macro-average HV in both settings, reaching 39.35 on ID benchmarks and 26.30 on OOD benchmarks. It also outperforms the strongest fixed-cardinality alternatives, with improvements of 0.28 HV points under ID conditions and 1.80 points under OOD conditions. These results are particularly noteworthy because the competing configurations are optimized separately for each benchmark, whereas PISA-E determines ensemble cardinality dynamically for individual prompts at inference time. The larger advantage under OOD conditions further highlights the benefits of adaptive cardinality when generalizing to previously unseen task groups.

The results also reveal differences across benchmarks. While adaptive cardinality improves HV in several cases, fixed-cardinality strategies remain competitive and occasionally outperform PISA-E. In particular, fixed k=1k=1 achieves higher HV on RouterBench in both settings, indicating that invoking additional models does not necessarily improve the trade-off for every task distribution. Nevertheless, the aggregate results suggest that ensemble cardinality is better treated as a prompt-dependent routing decision rather than a fixed configuration parameter, allowing additional model invocations to be allocated selectively according to predicted utility and inference-cost preferences.

4.5. Component Analysis

We analyze two components of PISA-E: the ensemble-success estimator used to select model subsets and the response resolver used to combine their outputs. For ensemble-success estimation, we compare the default Poisson-binomial (PB) formulation with a Gaussian-copula (GC) alternative that explicitly models dependencies among model correctness events. For response resolution, we consider standard BERTScore-based minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding, capability-weighted BERTScore variants, and pretrained or fine-tuned PairRanker. Standard BERTScore selects the response with the highest aggregate semantic similarity to the other ensemble responses. Other-weighted BERTScore weights the reference responses according to their estimated model capabilities, while self-weighted BERTScore additionally weights each candidate response by its own estimated capability. PairRanker instead employs a learned pairwise response-ranking model. Further details on the alternative estimator and resolvers are provided in the appendix.

Ensemble-Success Estimation.

We investigate the impact of the ensemble-success estimator by comparing PB and GC across different response resolvers. Table 6 reports task performance at α=1\alpha=1 under ID and OOD conditions. GC improves performance for several resolver configurations, particularly other-weighted BERTScore and PairRanker. However, these improvements do not consistently extend to self-weighted BERTScore, for which PB achieves higher macro-average performance in both ID (75.27% versus 75.23%) and OOD (63.24% versus 62.36%) settings. Overall, PB combined with self-weighted BERTScore achieves the highest aggregate performance, indicating that explicitly modeling correctness dependencies does not consistently improve ensemble performance and supporting the simpler PB formulation as the default estimator.

Ensemble Resolver Quality.

We further investigate how the choice of response resolver affects ensemble performance. As shown in Table 6, self-weighted BERTScore achieves the highest aggregate performance among the evaluated resolvers when paired with PB, outperforming standard BERTScore by 0.92 percentage points in ID and 1.21 percentage points in OOD settings. In contrast, PairRanker exhibits greater sensitivity to the ensemble-success estimator, with GC substantially improving performance over PB for both pretrained and fine-tuned variants. Fine-tuning consistently improves PairRanker performance over its pretrained counterpart under both estimation methods, although neither variant surpasses self-weighted BERTScore in aggregate performance. These findings support capability-weighted semantic similarity as an effective response resolution strategy and motivate self-weighted BERTScore as the default resolver in PISA-E.

4.6. Ablation of Prompt-Dependent Model Ranking

To assess the contribution of prompt-dependent model ranking, we compare PISA-E against a fixed-global baseline that retains adaptive ensemble cardinality but ranks models using their global training-set capabilities instead of prompt-specific estimates. This isolates the effect of prompt-dependent ranking while preserving the cost-aware ensemble selection framework. Table 7 shows that PISA-E improves macro-average HV by 4.96 points under ID conditions and 0.91 points under OOD conditions. It outperforms the fixed-global baseline on all four ID benchmarks and on Track-2 and RouterBench under OOD conditions, while the baseline performs better on FusionBench and SPROUT. Across all eight scenarios, PISA-E achieves a macro-average HV of 32.82 compared with 29.89 for the fixed-global baseline, indicating that prompt-dependent ranking contributes to cost–performance improvements independently of adaptive cardinality.

5. Related Work

Cost-Aware Model Routing

LLM routing selects a model for each prompt by estimating response quality and accounting for inference cost. EmbedLLM (Zhuang et al., 2025) learns latent representations from a model–question correctness matrix. Clustering-based methods instead use similarities among prompts to estimate model performance: UniRoute (Jitkrittum et al., 2026) and Avengers-PRO (Zhang et al., 2025c; Zhang et al., 2026) rely on hard cluster assignments and cluster-level statistics, while ZeroRouter (Yan et al., 2026) combines clustering with item response theory. PISA differs in using soft cluster memberships and model-specific predictors to estimate prompt-dependent capabilities. Related cost-aware inference strategies include LLM cascades (Chen et al., 2024; Dekoninck et al., 2025) and risk-aware routing (Hao et al., 2026). Cascades may escalate requests sequentially; PISA-E instead selects models for parallel execution before generating their responses.

LLM Ensembling and Response Aggregation

LLM ensembling combines responses from multiple models to exploit complementary capabilities. Aggregation methods include majority voting (Wang et al., 2023; Ai et al., 2026), learned ranking and fusion, as in LLM-Blender (Jiang et al., 2023) and URG (Lv et al., 2024), and similarity-based minimum Bayes risk decoding, including variants that account for uncertainty (Daheim et al., 2025). Multi-agent debate (Du et al., 2024) and Mixture-of-Agents (Wang et al., 2025) also combine model outputs, but involve interaction across successive rounds or stages. PISA-E does not organize such collaboration: after selecting an ensemble, it queries the models in parallel and resolves their responses using capability-weighted semantic similarity.

Adaptive and Cost-Aware Ensemble Selection

Ensemble selection determines which models to invoke, and whether that choice changes across queries. LLM-TOPLA (Tekin et al., 2024) and DFPE (Cohen et al., 2026) construct ensembles that are subsequently reused across queries, whereas SelectLLM (Maurya et al., 2025) adapts ensemble composition to the input while retaining a fixed cardinality. ThriftLLM (Huang et al., 2025) jointly adapts composition and cardinality under cost constraints, but addresses classification queries rather than open-ended response generation.

Other adaptive multi-model approaches make different inference decisions. EMS (Liu et al., 2026a) expands the set of invoked models sequentially; LightRouter (Zhang et al., 2025b) combines model selection with staged collaboration; and retrieval-based selection and response enhancement are investigated in (Tang et al., 2026). Query-specific agentic systems instead configure task plans, agents, or collaboration strategies (Su et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026; Hamid et al., 2026). PISA-E targets pre-inference selection of a parallel ensemble for response generation. It scores candidate subsets using a strict-majority surrogate constructed from prompt-dependent individual capability estimates, jointly selecting composition and cardinality under an explicit cost–quality preference without training ensemble-specific predictors.

6. Conclusion

We introduced PISA, a prompt-adaptive, cost-aware single-model router, and PISA-E, its extension to ensemble routing. Both methods use prompt-dependent capability estimates, which PISA-E reuses to jointly select ensemble composition and cardinality without ensemble-specific training. Across four heterogeneous benchmarks, PISA achieves the highest macro-average hypervolume among the evaluated single-model routers under both ID and OOD conditions. PISA-E achieves the highest macro-average task performance among the evaluated ensemble approaches, exceeding the strongest competitors by 2.09 and 2.87 percentage points, respectively, when prioritizing response quality. At selected lower-cost operating points, PISA-E also improves macro-average task performance while reducing average inference cost by approximately 36% under ID and 25% under OOD conditions. Component analyses and ablations support the contributions of capability-aware response resolution, prompt-dependent ranking, and adaptive ensemble cardinality. Together, these results demonstrate that a shared capability-estimation framework supports effective single-model routing and selective ensembling, with cost–quality preferences adjustable at inference time without retraining. For Web-based services such as search, recommendation, and intelligent agents, this flexibility offers a way to adapt inference expenditure to heterogeneous user requests and changing quality–cost preferences.

Appendix A Additional Experimental Details

Benchmarks and evaluation scores.

Table 8 summarizes the evaluated benchmarks. We use the original evaluation scores provided by each benchmark, which are all in the range [0,1][0,1]. FusionBench uses binary correctness, SPROUT employs LLM-judge scores, while RouterBench and Track-2 include task-dependent evaluation scores. Task performance is computed by averaging scores within each task group and then taking the macro-average across groups, consistently for all methods. For capability estimation, PISA derives binary success labels from the training scores using yi​m=𝟙[si​m≥0.5]y_{im}=\mathds{1}[s_{im}\geq 0.5] and trains model-specific predictors on these labels.

Data partitions.

For OOD evaluation, we construct group level partitions independently of the original benchmark splits. Entire task groups are assigned either to ID, which supplies training and validation data, or to OOD, which is reserved exclusively for testing. All available rows of held-out groups are used for OOD evaluation, irrespective of their original partition. The group assignments are selected without considering model outcomes, targeting approximately 20% of the available prompts for OOD evaluation, subject to a 30% upper bound. We require at least three OOD groups spanning three task categories and domains, and at least three retained ID groups. Among valid partitions, we select those closest to the target proportion. Table 9 reports the resulting assignments.

Experimental repetitions.

The five random seeds are 11, 22, 33, 44, and 55. Thus, reported standard deviations measure run-to-run variability under fixed data partitions.

Baselines.

DFPE follows its clustering and representative selection procedure, using global statistics fitted on ID training data when evaluating held-out OOD task groups. LLM-TOPLA constructs and prunes model teams following its original procedure. SelectLLM uses WeightedMaxConf, its best-performing configuration, with a RoBERTa-base multilabel classifier and inverse-square-root confidence weighted voting, following the original article. For PairRanker and MBR, fixed-size ensembles are formed from the top-kk models ranked by macro-average training performance.

Implementation Details.

For PISA, the maximum number of clusters and the soft-assignment parameter β\beta are selected using validation data. Cost–performance operating points are obtained by sweeping α\alpha from 0.10 to 1.00 in increments of 0.05.

Ensemble resolution.

We consider several alternatives to the self-weighted BERTScore resolver introduced in Section 3. Given an ensemble EE and its generated responses {yi}i∈E\{y_{i}\}_{i\in E}, standard minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding with BERTScore (Zhang* et al., 2020) selects the response maximizing its aggregate similarity to the ensemble outputs:

(18) SiMBR=∑j∈EBERTScore⁡(yi,yj).S_{i}^{\mathrm{MBR}}=\sum_{j\in E}\operatorname{BERTScore}(y_{i},y_{j}).

The other-weighted variant incorporates the prompt-dependent capability estimates produced by PISA:

(19) Siother=∑j∈Ewj​BERTScore⁡(yi,yj),S_{i}^{\mathrm{other}}=\sum_{j\in E}w_{j}\operatorname{BERTScore}(y_{i},y_{j}),

where wjw_{j} denotes the normalized capability estimate of the model generating response yjy_{j}. Unlike self-weighted BERTScore, other-weighted BERTScore does not additionally weight each candidate by its own estimated capability.

Inference costs.

Routing decisions use training-set average model costs, normalized as described in Section 3. Reported inference costs instead use the benchmark-recorded costs of individual responses, summed over all selected models and averaged across test queries. Models with missing responses still contribute their recorded inference costs. Local routing and response-resolution overhead are excluded.

Hypervolume metric.

We assess routing cost–performance trade-offs using normalized dominated hypervolume (HV) (Zitzler and Thiele, 1998). Let ℱ={(ci,pi)}i=1n\mathcal{F}=\{(c_{i},p_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} denote the non-dominated operating points ordered by increasing cost, with reference point r=(cref,pref)r=(c_{\mathrm{ref}},p_{\mathrm{ref}}). The dominated area is

(20) HVraw=∑i=1n(ci+1−ci)​(pi−pref),cn+1=cref,\mathrm{HV}_{\mathrm{raw}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(c_{i+1}-c_{i})(p_{i}-p_{\mathrm{ref}}),\qquad c_{n+1}=c_{\mathrm{ref}},

where only points within the reference bounds contribute. We normalize by

(21) HVnorm=HVrawcref​(1−pref).\mathrm{HV}_{\mathrm{norm}}=\frac{\mathrm{HV}_{\mathrm{raw}}}{c_{\mathrm{ref}}(1-p_{\mathrm{ref}})}.

The performance reference is the macro-average expected score of a uniformly random single-model router. The cost reference is defined as a percentile of the per-prompt full-model-pool inference cost distribution, computed separately for each benchmark and evaluation partition. We use the 40th percentile for single-model routing comparisons and the 70th percentile for ensemble-routing comparisons. The higher reference for ensemble routing accommodates the larger inference costs associated with querying multiple models. Within each comparison, the same reference point is used for all methods. Both reference coordinates remain fixed across methods, and HV values are multiplied by 100 when reported.

Appendix B Gaussian-Copula Model for Dependent Ensemble Success

The Poisson-binomial surrogate assumes conditional independence among model correctness events. To investigate whether modeling their dependencies improves ensemble selection, we consider a Gaussian-copula alternative.

For an ensemble EE of size kk, let p^m​(x)\hat{p}_{m}(x) denote the capability estimate provided by PISA for model mm. We introduce latent variables 𝐆E∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,RE)\mathbf{G}_{E}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},R_{E}), where RER_{E} is a correlation matrix, and define

(22) Bm(x)=𝟙[Gm≤Φ−1(p^m(x))],B_{m}(x)=\mathds{1}\left[G_{m}\leq\Phi^{-1}(\hat{p}_{m}(x))\right],

where Φ\Phi denotes the standard normal CDF. This construction preserves the marginal probabilities Pr⁡(Bm​(x)=1)=p^m​(x)\Pr(B_{m}(x)=1)=\hat{p}_{m}(x) while introducing dependencies through RER_{E}. The ensemble-success surrogate becomes

(23) p^EGC​(x)=Pr⁡(∑m∈EBm​(x)≥⌊k2⌋+1).\hat{p}^{\mathrm{GC}}_{E}(x)=\Pr\left(\sum_{m\in E}B_{m}(x)\geq\left\lfloor\frac{k}{2}\right\rfloor+1\right).

When RE=IR_{E}=I, the formulation reduces to the Poisson-binomial surrogate.

Dependence estimation.

We estimate a prompt-independent correlation matrix RR from training data using pairwise maximum likelihood, following the composite-likelihood approach to multivariate probit estimation (Ashford and Sowden, 1970). Let yi​m=𝟙[si​m≥0.5]y_{im}=\mathds{1}[s_{im}\geq 0.5] denote the observed binary correctness of model mm on training prompt ii, using the same threshold as PISA, and let p~i​m\tilde{p}_{im} denote its out-of-fold capability estimate. For each model pair (m,n)(m,n), the probability of joint correctness under latent correlation ρ\rho is

(24) π11(i)​(ρ)=Φ2​(Φ−1​(p~i​m),Φ−1​(p~i​n),ρ),\pi_{11}^{(i)}(\rho)=\Phi_{2}\left(\Phi^{-1}(\tilde{p}_{im}),\Phi^{-1}(\tilde{p}_{in});\rho\right),

where Φ2\Phi_{2} denotes the bivariate standard-normal CDF. The remaining outcome probabilities follow from the marginals: π10(i)=p~i​m−π11(i)\pi_{10}^{(i)}=\tilde{p}_{im}-\pi_{11}^{(i)}, π01(i)=p~i​n−π11(i)\pi_{01}^{(i)}=\tilde{p}_{in}-\pi_{11}^{(i)}, and π00(i)=1−p~i​m−p~i​n+π11(i)\pi_{00}^{(i)}=1-\tilde{p}_{im}-\tilde{p}_{in}+\pi_{11}^{(i)}. We estimate each correlation as

(25) ρ^m​n=arg⁡max⁡∑iρ∈(−1,1)⁡log⁡πyi​m​yi​n(i)​(ρ).\hat{\rho}_{mn}=\arg\max_{\rho\in(-1,1)}\sum_{i}\log\pi_{y_{im}y_{in}}^{(i)}(\rho).

The pairwise estimates are assembled into RR, with unit diagonal, and projected onto the nearest valid correlation matrix to ensure positive semidefiniteness.

Inference.

For each candidate ensemble, we extract the corresponding submatrix RER_{E} and approximate Eq. (23) using 2,048 Monte Carlo samples from 𝒩⁡(𝟎,RE)\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},R_{E}). The estimated success probability is the fraction of samples satisfying the strict-majority condition. This estimate replaces the Poisson-binomial surrogate in the PISA-E utility, leaving candidate construction, cost normalization, and ensemble selection unchanged.

Appendix C PISA Additional Experiments

C.1. Hypervolume Reference-Point Sensitivity

To assess the sensitivity of our results to the hypervolume reference point, we vary both its cost and performance coordinates. As described in Appendix A, the main experiments use fixed reference costs corresponding to the 40th and 70th percentiles of the full-pool cost distribution for single-model and ensemble routing, respectively. These reference points accommodate the operating points of the compared methods, while the reference performance corresponds to a uniformly random router. Although these choices provide a principled basis for comparison, HV values depend on the selected reference point. We therefore examine whether the aggregate advantage of PISA persists under alternative reference points. Figure 2 shows that PISA maintains a positive macro-average HV advantage over all competing single-model routers across the evaluated configurations. While the magnitude of this advantage varies with the reference coordinates, the relative ranking remains unchanged. These results indicate that the superior aggregate cost–performance trade-offs of PISA are not contingent on the specific reference point adopted in the main evaluation.

Appendix D PISA-E Additional Experiments

D.1. Hypervolume Reference-Point Sensitivity

We further examine whether the advantage of adaptive ensemble cardinality depends on the HV reference point selected for the main evaluation. Figure 3 reports the macro-average HV differences between PISA-E and each fixed-cardinality variant when varying the performance and cost references independently. Across all evaluated configurations, PISA-E maintains a positive HV advantage over every fixed-cardinality alternative. Although the magnitude of these differences varies with the reference coordinates, the aggregate ranking remains unchanged. The consistent advantage across reference configurations shows that the aggregate benefits of adaptive ensemble cardinality persist under different HV reference points.

D.2. Sensitivity to Maximum Ensemble Cardinality

Table 10 examines the effect of restricting the maximum ensemble cardinality kmaxk_{\max}. Under ID conditions, PISA-E achieves a macro-average HV of 39.35 with kmax=11k_{\max}=11, remaining competitive when the maximum cardinality is reduced, with HV reaching 39.41 at kmax=7k_{\max}=7. Under OOD conditions, allowing larger ensembles provides more substantial benefits, although restricting kmaxk_{\max} to seven still yields an HV of 26.07, compared with 26.30 when allowing up to eleven models. Thus, PISA-E retains strong aggregate cost–performance trade-offs under moderate restrictions on ensemble cardinality, while the larger gains observed under OOD conditions highlight the benefits of access to a broader range of ensemble sizes.

Appendix E Greedy Selection vs. Exhaustive Surrogate Optimization

We evaluate the greedy candidate-selection procedure by comparing it with exhaustive optimization of the ensemble-success surrogate. Both approaches use the same capability estimates, Poisson-binomial surrogate, and self-weighted BERTScore resolver, with kmax=7k_{\max}=7. Exhaustive optimization evaluates all feasible model subsets, requiring the assessment of ∑k=1kmax(Mk)\sum_{k=1}^{k_{\max}}\binom{M}{k} candidates for a pool of MM models. In contrast, greedy selection considers only ⌈kmax/2⌉\lceil k_{\max}/2\rceil odd-cardinality prefixes of the single-model utility ranking, substantially reducing the search space.

Figure 4 compares the cost–performance curves on Track-2 and RouterBench. Greedy selection achieves trade-offs comparable to exhaustive optimization, with closely aligned curves on Track-2 and favorable performance across several intermediate-cost regions on RouterBench. These results indicate that greedy ranking prefixes provide a computationally efficient alternative while maintaining competitive cost–performance trade-offs in the evaluated settings.
